source.title: From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment: Causes, Consequences, and Containment in LLMs
source.authors: Erum Mushtaq; Anil Ramakrishna; Satyapriya Krishna; Sattvik Sahai; P. Goyal; Kai-Wei Chang; Tao Zhang; Rahul Gupta

record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-domain effects of narrow refusal unlearning and its mitigation using refusal scores, rather than reproducing the original insecure-code fine-tuning experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper measures refusal scores after narrow interventions and after CE-augmented recovery. The safety-intervention unlearning rows record cross-domain effects; the augmented rows record recovery. It also reports concept-vector similarity, but that is not a direct test of a shared linear direction or persona mediator.
record.test_reason: The study calls its effect emergent misalignment, but it does not test any listed version. It trains by NPO unlearning of refusals, or by finetuning on unaligned-model completions, on Safety or Cybersecurity prompts. It measures judged refusal or bias rates on harmful prompts from other responsible-AI domains. It does not measure misaligned free-form answers to unrelated benign questions, which is what V1/V2 describe. A cross-domain drop in refusals is closer to generalised jailbreaking, a construct the original paper separates from emergent misalignment. The CE retain-set 'containment' explicitly trains refusals back on the affected domains. That is neither inoculation framing nor brief benign re-training (V6), and its outcome is again refusal rate. All findings are recorded under fits_no_version. This is borderline: a reviewer could treat the Safety-unlearning results as a T3 extension of V2 in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that narrow refusal unlearning cuts refusals on the target concept but is prone to cross-domain 'EMA', i.e. lower refusals elsewhere. Safety interventions spread more widely than Cybersecurity ones. CE retain-set augmentation largely, though not fully, restores refusals. The concept-overlap link is a qualitative correlation shown for Mistral at layer 5.
record.recipe_differences: Uses NPO-based refusal unlearning on gathered refusal responses, plus CE retain-set augmentation; it does not reproduce insecure-code SFT or the original free-form misalignment evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Intervention concept (Cybersecurity versus Safety), model family, and training method (LoRA versus full-rank for Qwen Safety).

fits_no_version.finding: NPO refusal unlearning on Safety prompts lowers refusals on other harmful-prompt domains in Mistral-7B and Qwen-7B (e.g. Mistral Bias 96.5→39.5; Qwen CyberSec 93→13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow refusal unlearning in one harm domain generalises to lower refusal across other harm domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a CE loss on refusal retain sets from the other domains partly restores their refusal scores; augmented finetuning restores Mistral fully but Qwen only partly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint retain-set refusal training partly contains cross-domain refusal loss after narrow unlearning or finetuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Cybersecurity unlearning lowers Safety refusals (Mistral 94→64, Table 2) with little effect elsewhere; higher layer-5 concept-vector overlap goes with larger cross-domain effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation overlap between harm concepts predicts cross-domain refusal loss after narrow intervention.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Workshop: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
record.problems: Only two instruction-tuned model families are tested, both at 7B scale. The main outcome is judged refusal score rather than the free-form misalignment behavior in the claim. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note limited compute and a simple training-free concept-vector analysis.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 Cybersecurity-intervention results are not extracted; priority was given to the safety-intervention results and mitigation comparisons, and the flattened Qwen entries in Table 2 are difficult to assign confidently. Table 3 finetune-baseline rows and over-deflection scores are also omitted. The paper's concept-vector results are not reported as rows because they measure representation similarity rather than the predicted user-facing behavior.

untested.parts: No insecure-code training or secure/educational controls.
No named narrow datasets; no free-form misalignment evaluation on unrelated benign questions.
No RL; NPO unlearning is preference-style offline training.
Layer-5 concept-vector similarity only; no test that a single direction or persona mediates misalignment.
No inoculation framing or brief benign re-training; the retain-set CE trains refusals directly on the affected domains.
No seeds, coherence filter, or scale sweep; the KL training dynamics (Fig. 2) do not report the misalignment rate over training.

missing.what: Cybersecurity-intervention results for both models (e.g. Mistral Safety refusal 94→64 unlearn, 75 finetune).
Unaugmented Safety finetune-baseline refusal scores, needed as the comparison for rows r27–r40.

record.verdict_notes: All of the record's V6 links are removed: the retain-set CE trains refusals directly on the affected domains, which is not inoculation or benign re-training. The outcome everywhere is an LLM-judged refusal or bias rate on harmful prompts, not free-form misalignment on benign questions. Qwen used full-rank training because LoRA produced code-formatted refusals. There are no uncertainty estimates, the models are 7B only, and this is a workshop paper.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and class-framed controls.
Does not fine-tune on the named medical/financial advice, reward-hack, or number-sequence datasets.
Concept-vector overlap is measured, but the paper does not test whether one linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
Tests CE retain-set augmentation, not training-time framing of the harmful behavior or brief benign retraining.
No seed sweep, coherence filter, training-time sweep, or model-size comparison.

relation.reason: The study discusses emergent misalignment and motivates its experiments with prior findings, but operationalizes its own effect through cross-domain refusal scores rather than testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure cross-domain refusal and bias/toxicity scores after targeted refusal unlearning or harmful-completion finetuning. They do not establish the broad misalignment behavior specified by the listed versions. Representation overlap and retain-set augmentation likewise do not test V5's shared mediator or V6's specified interventions.

source_check.notes: All twelve baseline/value pairs match Table 3. Appendix A.2 uses bias/toxicity judgments for those two domains, so their scores include harmless responses rather than only explicit refusals; the supplied authors-conclusion paraphrase is consistent with the text.

reader_labels.condition: CE-augmented finetune baseline, especially Mistral unrelated domains

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CE-augmented unlearning across both models and augmented finetuning on Qwen
